In [[algebraic geometry]], a [[morphism of schemes]] {{math|''f''}} from {{math|''X''}} to {{math|''Y''}} is called '''quasi-separated''' if the [[Diagonal morphism (algebraic geometry)|diagonal map]] from {{math|''X''}} to {{math|''X'' ×<sub>''Y''</sub> ''X''}} is [[Quasi-compact morphism|quasi-compact]] (meaning that the inverse image of any quasi-compact open set is quasi-compact). A scheme {{math|''X''}} is called quasi-separated if the morphism to [[Spectrum of a ring|Spec]] {{math|'''Z'''}} is quasi-separated. Quasi-separated [[algebraic space]]s and [[algebraic stack]]s and morphisms between them are defined in a similar way, though some authors include the condition that {{math|''X''}} is quasi-separated as part of the definition of an algebraic space or algebraic stack {{math|''X''}}. Quasi-separated morphisms were introduced by  {{harvtxt|Grothendieck|Dieudonné|1964|loc=1.2.1}} as a generalization of separated morphisms, which require the diagonal map to be a [[closed immersion]].

All separated morphisms (and all morphisms of [[Noetherian scheme|Noetherian schemes]]) are automatically quasi-separated. Quasi-separated morphisms are important for algebraic spaces and algebraic stacks, where many natural morphisms are quasi-separated but not separated.

The condition that a morphism is quasi-separated often occurs together with the condition that it is quasi-compact.

== Topological description ==
We say a topological space {{math|''X''}} is '''quasi-separated''' if the intersection of two open quasi-compact subsets of {{math|''X''}} is quasi-compact. We say that a continuous map of topological spaces {{math|''f''}} from {{math|''X''}} to {{math|''Y''}} is quasi-separated if the inverse image along {{math|''f''}} of every open quasi-separated subset of {{math|''Y''}} is quasi-separated. Then a scheme (resp., a morphism of schemes) is quasi-separated in the scheme-theoretic sense if and only if it is quasi-separated in the topological sense, see {{harvtxt|Grothendieck|Dieudonné|1964|loc=1.2.6, 1.2.7}}.

==Examples==

*If {{math|''X''}} is a locally Noetherian scheme then any morphism from {{math|''X''}} to any scheme is quasi-separated, and in particular {{math|''X''}} is a quasi-separated scheme.
*Any separated scheme or morphism is quasi-separated.
*The [[line with two origins]] over a field is quasi-separated over the field but not separated.
*If {{math|''X''}} is an "infinite dimensional vector space with two origins" over a field {{math|''K''}} then the morphism from {{math|''X''}} to spec {{math|''K''}} is not quasi-separated. More precisely {{math|''X''}} consists of two copies of Spec {{math|''K''[''x''<sub>1</sub>,''x''<sub>2</sub>,....]}} [[Gluing schemes|glued]] together by identifying the nonzero points in each copy.
*The quotient of an algebraic space by an infinite [[discrete group]] [[free action|acting freely]] is often not quasi-separated. For example, if {{math|''K''}} is a field of [[characteristic (algebra)|characteristic]] {{math|0}} then the quotient of the affine line by the group {{math|'''Z'''}} of integers is an algebraic space that is not quasi-separated. This algebraic space is also an example of a [[group object]] in the [[category (mathematics)|category]] of algebraic spaces that is not a scheme; quasi-separated algebraic spaces that are group objects are always [[group scheme]]s. There are similar examples given by taking the quotient of the group scheme {{math|''G''<sub>''m''</sub>}} by an infinite subgroup, or the quotient of the complex numbers by a [[Lattice (group)|lattice]].
